opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the agent paradigm changes what we should ask of an architecture. In the chatbot era, the main question was how smart the model is in a single turn. With agents, the model runs for a long time: it calls tools, reads long observations, writes code, gets feedback, and loops many times. So the bottleneck shifts toward long-context efficiency, KV cache cost, and inference throughput, not only raw capability per token.

From that angle, I think MA is a very reasonable direction. Its core value is that it makes long-context inference much cheaper without giving up too much quality. For agents this matters a lot. If every step of a trajectory carries a huge context and the memory cost grows linearly and expensively, you can't afford long horizons, many parallel rollouts, or large-scale RL. Architecture efficiency directly decides how much exploration you can do, both in training and at deployment.

That said, I'd be careful not to over-romanticize any one architecture. Architecture sets the ceiling on efficiency, but what an agent actually does well still depends mostly on data, on the RL environments, and on whether the model learns to use its context well. Being able to fit a long context isn't the same as being able to reason over it. So for me, MA is an important piece of infrastructure. It makes the agent paradigm economically viable. But the real competition will be in how you train the model to plan, recover from mistakes, and use tools over long horizons.

If I had to summarize: for agents, efficiency itself becomes a form of intelligence, because cheaper inference means more thinking, more trials, and more feedback. MA fits that trend well, and I expect the architecture and the training paradigm to co-evolve even more tightly from here.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd start by saying that the agent paradigm changes what we actually ask of an architecture. In the chat era, the bottleneck was mostly knowledge and reasoning per response. In the agent era, the bottleneck becomes long-horizon context: you're running hundreds of tool calls, the context grows to hundreds of thousands of tokens, and most of the cost is in decoding and KV cache rather than in a single forward pass. So when I assess an architecture for agents, I look at three things: how it scales with context length, how cheap each step is at inference, and whether it preserves the kind of precise retrieval that an agent needs to not lose track of what it did fifty steps ago.

From that angle, I think the mixed or hybrid attention direction is the right bet, but not as a replacement for full attention, rather as a composition. Pure linear or state-space layers are very attractive on paper because the state is constant-size, but in practice they degrade on exact recall, and agents are brutally punished for exact recall failures. You forget a file path or a variable name and the whole trajectory collapses. So what we've found works is interleaving: a majority of layers with cheap local or sliding-window attention, and a smaller number of global full-attention layers that act as the memory backbone. The global layers are expensive, so you keep them sparse, and you can share or compress their KV cache. That gives you most of the throughput gain while keeping the model's ability to reach back precisely.

The other dimension is MoE, which I consider almost non-negotiable now for agent workloads. Agents need breadth, coding, tool use, reasoning across domains, and MoE lets you carry that breadth without paying for all of it on every token. The thing to be careful about is that agent decoding tends to be bursty and batch sizes are uneven, so expert load balancing and routing stability matter more than they did for chat.

So my honest assessment is: the architecture is necessary but not sufficient. A good hybrid attention plus MoE design maybe gives you a two to four times efficiency gain on long trajectories, and that's real money. But the harder problems in agents today are still on the training side, the reinforcement learning environments, the reward design, the long-horizon credit assignment. If I had to allocate effort, I'd put more into those than into further architectural novelty. The architecture just has to not get in the way.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with what the agent actually needs from the model. It’s not just answering a question; it’s taking an action, observing the result, and deciding what to do next. So I would assess MA by whether it supports that loop reliably and efficiently.

Can it preserve relevant information over a long task? Can it revise a plan when a tool returns something unexpected? And what does it cost to complete the task successfully? A model might look strong on individual responses but become expensive or unreliable when you run it through many steps.

I’d want to clarify what you mean by MA before making a specific architectural judgment. But my broader view is that the agent paradigm changes the unit of evaluation: we should care about the whole task, including recovery from mistakes, rather than just the quality of the next response.

sol-6.1.text:
If by MA you mean a multi-agent architecture, I’d assess it by asking what the additional agents actually contribute. Dividing a task among several agents can help when the work can be done independently, or when one agent can meaningfully check another. But adding agents also introduces communication costs, coordination problems, and more opportunities for errors to propagate.

I’d also distinguish the architecture of the underlying model from the architecture of the agent system. Giving a model several roles doesn’t necessarily give it stronger reasoning or better judgment. The underlying model still needs to understand the task, use tools reliably, and recognize when it has made a mistake.

So I would compare a multi-agent system with a strong single-agent baseline under the same budget. Does it complete more tasks successfully? Can it recover from failures? Does the improvement justify the latency and cost? For me, those results would determine whether MA is a useful architecture for the agent paradigm.
